meta.title: FaithWall vs Pray.com: The Lock-Screen Layer vs. the All-in-One App
meta.description: FaithWall vs Pray.com: one keeps Scripture free on your lock screen, the other is a paid all-in-one prayer, sleep, and Bible app. Which to pick, and why.

sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: **FaithWall vs Pray.com** comes down to layer vs. library. Pray.com is a paid all-in-one Christian app — prayer audio, sleep stories, daily devotionals, and a full Bible — with most of its library behind a **$69.99-a-year** Premium tier. **FaithWall** puts today's verse on your lock screen automatically, free, with no subscription at all. Different jobs, so most people comparing the two end up adding FaithWall regardless of what they do with Pray.com.

sections.text: If you're weighing **faithwall vs pray.com**, you've probably already seen Pray.com's ad — a celebrity narrator reading a bedtime story, a prayer-request wall, a full year of Bible readings, all bundled into one subscription. It's a lot of app. **FaithWall** does none of that. It does one thing: it keeps today's verse on your lock screen, automatically, without you opening anything. That's not a smaller version of what Pray.com does — it's a different job entirely, and it's the reason people who already pay for Pray.com still install FaithWall next to it.
What each app is actually for

Pray.com has grown into one of the largest prayer apps on the App Store, with over 17 million users. The free tier includes Pray Radio, daily prayer audio, podcasts, a prayer-request wall, and the plain text of the Bible. Premium — $69.99 a year or $9.99 a month, family plans available — unlocks the full sleep-story catalog, family devotionals, a guided Bible-in-a-year track, and ad-free playback. It's built to be opened and sat with: pick an episode, listen, close the app. FaithWall is built for the opposite motion. Pick a verse pack once, and it installs a rotating Scripture wallpaper on your lock screen through iOS Focus modes — no subscription, no app to remember to reopen.
Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.

Pray.com earns its size. The production quality is real — professional narration, a genuinely large sleep-story catalog, and a prayer-request feature that gives community intercession a home most apps skip entirely. For someone who wants one app to cover audio devotionals, a kids' Bible track, and a nightly wind-down routine, it's a reasonable single subscription instead of three separate ones. The catch is the one every all-in-one app shares: most of what makes it worth paying for sits behind Premium, and Premium is a recurring charge that has to keep earning its place on your card statement every single year.

**FaithWall** never asks for a card. It keeps today's verse on the one surface you check without deciding to — you unlock your phone dozens of times a day, and FaithWall turns a slice of those glances into Scripture instead of a notification pile. Nearly six in ten people (**59.9%**) carry at least one paid subscription going unused each month, averaging 2.6 of them, per Self Financial's 2026 survey. FaithWall was built to never become one of those: it's free, it installs the wallpaper itself, and the themed packs — Anxiety, Strength, Gratitude, Grief — mean you don't have to already know which verse today calls for.
Line up **faithwall vs pray.com** side by side and the shape of the difference is clear:

items: **What it does:** Pray.com is an all-in-one app — audio prayer, sleep stories, kids' content, a full Bible. FaithWall is daily Scripture on the lock screen, nothing else.
**How you use it:** Pray.com is something you open and listen to, usually for ten minutes or more. FaithWall runs in the background — nothing to open, nothing to finish.
**Price:** Pray.com's core library is free; the sleep catalog, family devotionals, and Bible-in-a-year track sit behind $69.99/year Premium. FaithWall is free, full stop, with no premium tier.
**The habit risk:** Pray.com depends on you remembering to open an app and press play. FaithWall depends on you unlocking your phone, which happens whether you remember or not.
**iOS integration:** Pray.com sends a push notification asking you to come back. FaithWall installs the wallpaper directly via Focus modes — nothing to tap, nothing to remember.

sections.text: Here's the mistake people make trying to get both jobs out of one app. They screenshot a verse from Pray.com's Bible reader and set it as their wallpaper by hand. It looks fine for a few days. Then the crop sits wrong behind the clock widget, and by week two they're back to a photo of the dog. An audio-and-reading app was never designed for the lock-screen surface — its images are built to be looked at inside the app, not glanced at for half a second from across a room. That's the exact gap **FaithWall** was built to close: no screenshotting, no manual re-crop, just a pack that installs itself and keeps rotating on its own.

sections.content: If you're already paying for Pray.com and wondering whether to keep it, add FaithWall first. It's free and takes 60 seconds, and it tells you fast whether you actually miss the lock-screen piece once it's covered.

sections.text: For most people comparing **faithwall vs pray.com**, the honest answer isn't either-or. Start with FaithWall — free, 60 seconds, no subscription to remember to cancel later. Keep Pray.com if you specifically want the sleep stories, the prayer-request wall, or a guided Bible-in-a-year track with narration; those are real features FaithWall doesn't attempt. If you're weighing the wider prayer-app field first, our [best prayer app for iPhone](/blog/best-prayer-app-for-iphone) guide ranks Pray.com's category against Hallow, Echo Prayer, and PrayerMate. And if it's specifically Catholic-leaning guided sessions you're after rather than Pray.com's broadly evangelical tone, [FaithWall vs Hallow](/faithwall-vs-hallow) covers that same always-on-vs-session trade-off.

sections.content: Pray.com and FaithWall aren't really competing for the same ten minutes of your day. One is a library you visit on purpose. The other is a line of Scripture you see without trying to. Paying for the first doesn't cover the second — and the second doesn't need you to pay for anything.
